newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US Nov CPI seen drawing modest concern.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US Nov CPI seen drawing modest concern.

text.p: Creeping growth in U.S. consumer prices should not snowball into a sustained inflation bubble -- for now, analysts said.
But if the consumer price index (CPI) continues to rise at its current monthly rate of 0.3-percent, inflation pressures will again begin to worry economists and Federal Reserve officials, they noted.

"Basically, since July inflation has dropped lower on the list of financial market concerns, but I firmly predict at some point in the foreseeable future, inflation is again going to be a worry," said Ken Mayland at Society National Bank.
Mayland, Society's chief economist, said he sees upward pressure in the form of higher wages and apparel prices in the months ahead.
"My view of the economy is a little firmer than the financial markets give it credit. My gut tells me the (inflation) risks are to the higher side of forecasts," Mayland added.
Inflation-watchers will get a fresh reading on consumer price trends when the Labor Department releases the November CPI report on Thursday, December 12 at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
A Reuters poll produced consensus forecasts for a gain of 0.3 percent in overall CPI in November, while the core rate, excluding volatile food and energy components, was seen rising 0.2 percent.
Those forecasts mirror the actual CPI readings from October.
On Wednesday the Labor Department reported the producer price index rose 0.4 percent in November, largely as a result of a 2.8 percent rise in gasoline prices. The core rate rose only 0.1 percent.

CPI has behaved remarkably well during the current U.S. expansion that began over six years ago. Annual CPI has actually held below 3.0 percent since 1992, but on a trailing 12-month basis, CPI stood right at 3.0 in October.
Some analysts expect CPI to break above 3.0 percent in the months to come.

Nikko Securities International chief economist Robert Brusca notes that while the last three CPI reports yielded a 2.6 percent annualized rate, and 2.7 percent on the core rate, the 1996 year-to-date figures are 3.2 percent overall and 2.8 percent on the core.
"The inflation news is already deteriorating, principally through wage increases," said Brusca.
In the November U.S. payrolls report released December 6, the Labor Department reported U.S. average hourly earnings stood at $11.99, up 40 cents, or 3.5 percent from a year earlier.
Fed officials, notably Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern, have repeatedly mentioned wage gains as a potential harbinger of faster future inflation.
"The Fed is probably going to have to raise interest rates by the first quarter of 1997. Inflation is building and the Fed is going to have to pay attention to it," Brusca said.
But other analysts remain more sanguine on inflation.

UBS Securities money market analyst Kathy Bostjancic said she does not see the Fed raising rates at all in 1997, with relatively modest gross domestic product growth and only minor futher wage gains ahead.
Bostjancic cited the third-quarter employment cost index, which showed wages and salaries rising just 0.6 percent, and 3.2 percent year-over-year.
"Wages will remain moderate and I don't see any upward pressure in the pipeline that would push up finished goods or consumer goods prices" Bostjancic said.
